title: El Salvador - Santa Ana Balam Washed
description:
Balam is a coffee built around the classic El Salvador flavor profile: sweet, balanced, comforting. Sourced from smallholder producers in Santa Ana in an effort to produce a consistent, high-quality washed coffee from one of El Salvador’s most established growing regions. The name Balam means “jaguar” in the Indigenous Maya language.
This is the kind of coffee we’d like to have around all the time if we could. It starts with rich chocolate sweetness but there’s just enough soft citrus like acidity to keep the cup clear. The overall impression is mellow and sweet. The result is clean, chocolatey, and familiar without feeling flat a coffee that works just as well black as it does with milk. In fact it pulls a great espresso shot as it does filter.
This washed coffee is made up of Bourbon, Caturra, Pacas, and Pacamara varieties, producing a delicious and familiar cup.

title: El Carmelo Reserve
description:
Oscar Osorio Henao grew up in a coffee family in Sonsón, Antioquia, Colombia, where his family has been farming coffee for more than 50 years. Oscar took a different path for a while, when he left the farm and spent eight years working in the textile industry. Eventually he returned to agriculture with his wife during the pandemic. That brought him back to coffee, and into the world of specialty coffee. Since then, Oscar has been learning what his farm can do.
This coffee comes from his El Carmelo farm and starts with Castillo, a workhorse Colombian variety known for its productivity and resilience. What makes it special is what happens after the cherries are picked. Oscar ferments the whole coffee cherry for 120 hours, five full days before depulping it and carefully drying the coffee. That is a long fermentation time. And it is not being done to just make the coffee taste funky.
The result is remarkably clean with lively fruit notes and generous sweetness and a little chocolate at the end giving the whole thing some balance.
Oscar is still relatively new to specialty coffee. He is experimenting with fermentation, learning what works on his farm, and planting varieties like Geisha and Wush Wush for the future. The Castillo in your cup today is one result of that experimentation. We like all this.
What makes coffee special is tasting what a farmer figures out in real time and getting to be part of the journey. Some coffees are interesting because of where they come from. Others are interesting because of what the producer is doing with them. Oscar Red Honey is both.
October's Monthly Drop is Oscar Red Honey. Give it a try while we’ve got it.

title: Colombia - Tabi Washed
description:
Génova native Leonid Ramirez has dedicated much of his life to coffee. Raised in a traditional coffee-growing family in one of Colombia’s most renowned coffee regions, he developed a deep connection to the land and the craft from an early age. After the loss of his father during childhood, Leonid began working to help support his family, taking on work as a chapolero (coffee picker) while still attending school. Those early experiences in the fields gradually grew into a lasting passion for coffee cultivation and production, shaping the path he continues to follow today.
In 2003, Leonid purchased his own farm, Cortina de Hierro, a 4-hectare property sitting at nearly 1900 meters above sea level in the hills of Génova. The farm is planted with traditional Colombian varieties including Caturra and Castillo, with shade trees spread throughout the property.
From the beginning, Leonid focused on improving the health of the farm and the quality of the coffee. He removed eucalyptus trees that were depleting the soil, renewed older coffee trees, and gradually invested in better farming and processing practices. Those efforts helped his coffees gain recognition in regional specialty coffee auctions and quality competitions.
Since 2016, Leonid has partnered closely with our friends at Cofinet deepening his work in specialty coffee through innovative processing and experimental fermentation techniques. Together, they’ve continued to push quality and consistency forward, helping shape the distinctive character his coffees are known for today. What stands out most about Leonid’s coffee is the steady commitment behind it. Decades of experience, careful farm management, and a willingness to keep improving have made Cortina de Hierro a respected producer in the region. Cortina de Hierro is very much a family operation. Leonid works alongside his uncle and cousins, who help oversee the day-to-day work across the farm.
At Big Shoulders, our goal is simple: roast the coffee in a way that lets Leonid’s work speak for itself. Careful roast development highlights the coffee’s sweetness, balance, and complexity while preserving the character built through farming and processing at Cortina de Hierro. The result is a clean, expressive cup that reflects both the quality of the farm and the care taken in roasting.
Despite all the attention to details that specialty coffee requires, Leonid still enjoys coffee the traditional way, a simple tinto sweetened with panela after a long day of work on the farm.

title: Panama Natural Red Bourbon
description:
Bambito Estate Coffee has been a family run farm since 1945. Alberto Sitton Rios acquired the farm from his father in the mountains of Chiriqui Province, Panama and has kept it a family business ever since- it's now in its fourth and fifth generation! Bambito Estate won the Best of Panama competition in 2021. This competition presents the opportunity for local estates to promote the quality of their harvests and is 100% designed and organized by the Specialty Coffee Association of Panama.
This Natural Red Bourbon boasts aromas of wild berries with a sweet taste that will brighten your senses! For exotic coffee lovers, this is an option that will leave you speechless.
*Available only as 10oz bags!

title: Guatemala
description:
This is the kind of coffee we love to drink every day. Sweet and balanced, but still interesting enough to keep your attention. This is a blend that comes from the highlands of Guatemala, pulling together coffees from Huehuetenango, San Marcos, and Nuevo Oriente. These are regions that consistently produce clean, high-grown coffees with great structure.
Our importing partner in Guatemala stays close to the producers, many of whom have been growing coffee for generations. The focus is simple: buy good coffee, handle it right, and keep it consistent without losing its origin. The coffees are washed, fermented for about 24 hours, and patio dried for a little over a week. It shows clean in the cup.
What you get is a coffee that’s very sweet up front, with some light fruit character and a clean finish. It’s approachable without being flat, and it holds up whether you’re pulling espresso or brewing a pot at home. This is the kind of profile we want behind the bar and in your kitchen, something you don’t have to think too hard about, but still very much appreciate when drinking it.

title: Wilton Benitez - Thermal Shock Red Bourbon
description:
This Red Bourbon from Wilton Benítez is one of the best coffees we’ve ever tasted.
Benitez works in Piendamó, Cauca, Colombia, where his family’s Granja Paraíso 92 has become the home base for an unusually ambitious approach to coffee processing. His background is a big part of the story. Benítez trained as a chemical engineer before returning his attention to coffee, and that experience has clearly influenced the way he approaches fermentation and processing.
At Granja Paraíso 92, coffee is treated with an incredible level of precision. The operation includes microbiology and quality-control laboratories alongside its processing facilities, allowing Benítez and his team to closely manage the conditions surrounding fermentation and drying. Temperature, pH, sugar concentration, time, and microorganisms can all become variables in the process. The goal isn't simply to make a coffee more intense or more fermented. It's to understand the character of the coffee you're starting with and use processing to reveal something compelling within it.
This lot starts with Red Bourbon, a variety prized for its sweetness, structure, and fruit character. From there, Benítez applies his Thermal Shock processing, using a controlled change in water temperature as part of the washing stage, and the cup is extraordinary.
What comes at you with red berry fruit and the sweet-tart snap of a Jolly Rancher. It's bright, juicy, and almost electric, but somehow remains incredibly refreshing. The acidity gives it lift, the sweetness keeps it grounded, and the whole party manages to be both intensely expressive and remarkably clean. That balance is difficult to achieve.
There is a tremendous amount of technique behind this coffee, but you don't need to understand the fermentation protocol to appreciate it. You just need to take a sip. For us, this is a joy ride of a coffee and one of the best we've ever tasted.
*Due to limited inventory, we are only listing Wilton Benitez as whole bean. If you do need your coffee ground, please leave a note a check out or email information@bigshoulderscoffee.com*

title: Honduras Finca Adolfo - Anaerobic Natural
description:
Bryan Adolfo Bautista Zelaya is the third generation of his family to grow coffee at Finca Adolfo in Marcala, Honduras. While coffee has been cultivated on the land for more than fifty years, Bryan has helped redefine what the farm is capable of. After graduating from university in 2017, he inherited a portion of the family farm at a time when Honduras was grappling with coffee leaf rust and historically low market prices. Faced with uncertainty, Bryan chose to pursue quality.
Working alongside his father, Juan Adolfo, his mother, Maria Dolores, and agronomists from IHCAFE, Bryan began producing carefully crafted microlots that highlighted the unique character of their farm. The results spoke for themselves. In just a few years, the family shifted their focus entirely to specialty coffee, investing in thoughtful farming practices and innovative processing methods. Bryan has since earned Honduras' Five Star Cupping Certification and continues to push the boundaries of fermentation, constantly refining his approach to produce coffees with greater clarity, complexity, and expression.
Finca Adolfo sits between 1,400 and 1,540 meters above sea level in the mountains of Marcala, where cool nights and warm days allow cherries to mature slowly and develop exceptional sweetness. The farm includes eleven productive hectares and a protected hectare of native forest surrounding a natural spring, a reminder that producing great coffee begins with caring for the land. Once planted exclusively with Lempira, the farm now grows Bourbon, Catuai, Pacamara, Parainema, and Gesha, each selected for its potential to express the farm's unique terroir.
This particular lot showcases Bryan's thoughtful approach to processing. Ripe Bourbon and Catuai cherries undergo a carefully managed 96-hour anaerobic fermentation in sealed bags before drying as a natural. The extended fermentation amplifies fruit sweetness and aromatic complexity while maintaining remarkable balance and a clean finish.
In the cup, vibrant blackberry sweetness takes the lead, layered with delicate jasmine florals and a bright, refined acidity. The natural process brings a silky texture and lingering sweetness, yet the coffee remains remarkably clean and transparent. It's a coffee with plenty of character, but one that never loses its sense of balance.
Bryan represents a new generation of Honduran producers who are honoring their family's legacy while writing its next chapter. Through careful farming, thoughtful experimentation, and a commitment to quality, he's producing coffees that showcase just how exciting Honduran coffee can be and we're proud to share this one with you.

title: Ethiopia Natural
description:
We’re always looking for coffees that carry both unmistakable flavor and a story to share. This lot from
Ethiopia
Natural – Kossa Geshe, Jimma Zone, Oromia
 delivers both.
Grown in the highlands of the Kebena Forest in Limmu Kossa, this coffee comes from producer Abdulwahid Sherif, whose work has quickly gained recognition. His 1,000-hectare farm, established to help protect one of the country’s last remaining dense forest regions, has, in less than ten years, risen to national and international acclaim. After taking over operations in 2016, Abdul’s coffees earned a Good Food Award just two years later, announcing the arrival of a standout producer from a region not traditionally in the spotlight.
What makes this coffee truly compelling goes beyond awards. Abdul has continually reinvested in both quality and community, expanding drying infrastructure, refining processing methods, and implementing meaningful worker support systems, including education initiatives and transparent wages. It’s a level of care that shows up clearly in the cup.
Processed naturally and grown at 1,800 meters, this lot is composed of classic
Ethiopia
n varieties (74110, 74140, 74112, and 74166), delivering a vibrant and layered profile. Expect a fruit-forward experience with notes of ripe strawberry and cherry, balanced by deeper tones of plum and dark chocolate, with a subtle lift of ginger on the finish.
Ethiopia
 is the birthplace of coffee, and its coffees remain among the most expressive in the world.
Ethiopia
 Natural – Kossa Geshe, Jimma Zone, Oromia
 is a reminder of why, offering both a vivid sense of place and the unmistakable imprint of a producer dedicated to pushing quality forward.  We’re excited to bring Abdul’s coffee back into our lineup.

title: Costa Rica - SL-28 White Honey
description:
This one’s all about that easy, toffee-like sweetness right up front. You’ll get some cooked fruit, a little raisin hanging in the background, and just enough bright, tart acidity to keep it from getting too heavy. It finishes kind of candy-corn sweet. Clean and super satisfying.
El Venado is a small, family-run setup in Grecia, out in Costa Rica’s West Valley. It’s run by brothers Alexander and Magali Delgado and their families, and they’ve really put in the work over the years planting a bunch of different varieties like SL-28, Bourbon, Caturra, Catuai, all to keep quality high and the farms healthy long-term.
The farms are all right next to each other, split into smaller lots so they can make clear observations. Then the mill’s just a few miles away at their home, so once they pick the cherries, they can get them processed the same day. Having the mill on site makes a difference in speed, efficiency and quality.
They do a few different processing styles, but this one’s a White Honey, which means they leave some of the fruit (mucilage) on the seed while it dries, which is where you get that balance of nice sweetness, a little brightness, and a very approachable cup overall.
This lot is SL-28, grown between 1200–1900 meters, and harvested during Costa Rica’s main season, December through April. Just a really solid, well-put-together coffee from people who clearly care about what they’re doing.

title: Wilder Lazo-Pink Bourbon-60 Hour Anaerobic Honey
description:
Wilder Lazo didn’t begin as a coffee producer. He’s actually a trained veterinarian with a specialty in livestock farming. But in 2016, when coffee prices fell and his father became seriously ill, Wilder returned home to the family farm in Colombia. Together with his brother, he took on the work of rebuilding it.
At first, their coffee cupped in the low 80s. Good, but Wilder knew they could do better. So he leaned into what he knew: science, care, and observation. He started testing soil samples, adjusting pH levels, and applying nutrients in precise doses to unlock the full potential of the land. He calls it precision agriculture. We call it brilliant.
That same level of precision and attention extends to every part of his process. This lot of Pink Bourbon underwent 60 hours of anaerobic fermentation. The slower pace lets the coffee’s natural character shine. Then it’s dried with the mucilage intact, finishing as a red honey process. The result? A fruit-forward cup that’s sweet, vibrant, and clean, and more of everything we love.
This coffee is a reminder that great things happen when people care, deeply, for their land, their family, and their craft.

title: Finca Bella Alejandria - Geisha
description:
Wilder Lazo never planned on building a career in coffee. He came back to it because things were falling apart. By 2016, coffee prices across Colombia were collapsing, and at the same time his father became seriously ill. Wilder had trained as a veterinarian focused on livestock, not coffee agronomy. But when the family needed help, he returned home to Huila alongside his brother to keep the farm alive and figure out why years of hard work still weren’t producing coffees that truly stood out.
At the time, their coffees were landing in the low 80s on the cupping table despite increasingly complicated processing experiments. Like much of the industry, they had started believing processing alone could create quality. Instead of chasing fermentation trends, he approached the farm the way he understood biology: as a complete living system. He started with the soil.
He began pulling detailed soil samples throughout the property, mapping nutrient deficiencies, correcting pH imbalances, and rebuilding microbial activity through what he now describes as precision agriculture. The idea was straightforward. If the trees themselves lacked the nutrition to develop exceptional fruit, no amount of clever processing would ever make up for weak raw material.
But for Wilder, improving cup quality only raised a bigger question: what was the absolute best expression of Gesha his farm could produce?
At La Dinastía, high in the mountains of Huila, he began cupping Gesha one tree at a time. Not by lot. Not by section. Individual trees.
Patterns slowly emerged. Some trees consistently produced softer, sweeter profiles with a vanilla-like texture. Others leaned heavily toward tropical fruit. But one phenotype kept separating itself from everything else around it: taller trees producing intensely floral coffees layered with jasmine, citrus blossom, and a level of aromatic complexity that he fell in love with.
Wilder began harvesting seeds only from those specific trees the most floral, the most elegant, the clearest expression of what he believed Gesha could become. Entire sections of the farm were replanted at elevations approaching 2,100 meters above sea level. Later, he established Bella Alejandría using seedlings sourced entirely from those carefully selected mother trees.
Over years of patient selection, propagation, and observation, the project evolved into what he now calls “Pure Genetics.”
This particular coffee happened almost by accident. After processing a larger batch of lemongrass co-fermented Gesha, another lot somehow picked up subtle traces of those aromatics during production possibly through shared fermentation infrastructure, though Wilder still isn’t entirely certain how it occurred. What makes the result so compelling is that the lemongrass character never feels imposed on the cup. It integrates naturally into the coffee’s structure, amplifying qualities that already exist within the variety itself: jasmine, bergamot, citrus blossom, and the tea-like

title: Sebastian Ramirez - Pink Bourbon
description:
From the misty hills of El Placer,
Sebastian
Ramirez
is redefining what washed coffee can be. A third-generation producer,
Sebastian
is known for blending deep respect for tradition with an experimental mindset, constantly refining fermentation and processing to elevate clarity and expression in the cup. El Placer has become a benchmark farm in the region, celebrated for meticulous lot separation, sustainability, and a relentless focus on quality.
This Washed Pink Bourbon showcases
Sebastian
’s precision at every step. Carefully harvested at peak ripeness and washed to preserve purity, the coffee reveals a vibrant yet elegant profile floral aromatics, silky sweetness, and a crisp, transparent finish that lets the variety shine. Pink Bourbon’s natural complexity is amplified here, offering both structure and nuance with every sip.
Clean, expressive, and deeply intentional, this coffee is a standout for anyone who values origin-driven flavor. Whether brewed as a delicate pour-over or a refined espresso,
Sebastian
Ramirez
’s El Placer Pink Bourbon delivers a memorable experience one that speaks to craftsmanship, innovation, and the future of Colombian coffee.

title: Myanmar-SL-28 Natural
description:
This coffee comes out of Mandalay, Myanmar which isn’t an origin you see every day. And that’s part of what makes it interesting. It’s an origin that is still developing, finding its footing, but done right, there’s measurable upside.
Shwe Yi Mon Estate sits around 1,000–1,150 meters above sea level.  They’re working with the land, not just pushing for yield. Coffee is interplanted with macadamia and hardwood shade trees, slowing maturation, building density in the cherry, and achieving character in the cup.
There’s also a lot of intention behind the farming. You see spacing trials, different shade strategies, and practical systems like drip irrigation paired with solar drying. It’s thoughtful.  Trying to improve year over year.
What’s a little unusual and worth calling out is that they’re growing SL28, a traditional Kenyan hybrid. You don’t typically see that here. My guess is it’s tied to disease resistance or adaptability. Either way, it’s a sign that they’re experimenting and not just following the "how we've  always done it" script.
The estate is run by U Ye Myint, who’s been in agriculture for decades. He studied agronomy and went on to found the Myanmar Coffee Association. He’s not just producing coffee, he’s helping build the foundation for the entire sector.
On the processing side, they're into naturals. Fruit dries on the seed, and when that’s handled well, you get more fruit expression, more sweetness, and a little bit of wildness in the cup. They’re selective in picking and disciplined in sorting before drying.
Drying happens on raised beds inside solar dryers over 18–25 days, slow enough to develop flavor, controlled enough to avoid defects.
Myanmar as a whole is still early compared to places like Ethiopia or Colombia, but producers like this are pushing it forward with curiosity. There’s alos investment. You can taste this in the cup.

title: El Yolombo Chiroso - Colombia
description:
This Colombian coffee hits right away with bright, tropical fruit, think passionfruit up front, followed by some light florals and a little lemongrass in the mix. As it cools the body becomes syrupy with notes of caramel. The acidity is refreshing. Crisp and clean, not sharp, and it rounds out with a soft, velvety body. It’s got a lot going on, but it’s still super drinkable. Just a really nice, clear cup.
This comes from Liliana Ramírez in Anzá, Antioquia. Small farm, less than a hectare, around 1,000 plants. A friend tipped us off, we got a sample roasted, and that was it. Quality was obvious right away.
Liliana processes everything the traditional way, using what’s called “3 cochadas.” She picks over three days, Monday through Wednesday. Floats and pulps each day, then combines it all and washes it together on Thursday. It’s simple, it works, and it fits the scale she’s working at. She does the basics like, consistent sorting and drying really well and that shows up in the cup.
100% Chiroso, grown at 1,850 meters, harvested January 2026. Straightforward in approach, but the cup says a lot.

title: Jorge Rojas - Chiroso Natural
description:
We like to say coffee tells a story, if you’re willing to listen.
This one starts in Planadas, Tolima, with
Jorge
Rojas
.
Jorge
was just 12 when his father passed away. While most kids were still in school,
Jorge
was shoulder to shoulder with his mother on their family’s coffee farm. He left school after third grade but he never stopped learning. He just learned a different way: through soil, rain, fruit, and patience.
He joined the ASOPEP association early on and leaned into organic, ecological farming. Together with 300 other farmers, he earned a BIO certification, making him one of the rare producers of organic high-end specialty coffee in Colombia.
This particular lot, awarded 94 points by Coffee Review, is Chiroso, a wild, beautiful variety that traces its roots to Ethiopia, though it was discovered in the town of Urrao, Antioquia. “Chiroso” means “bumpy” or “big” a nod to the lumpy shape of the achira cookie it resembles. The variety’s flavor is just as wild: bright tropical fruit, delicate florals, and a spicy cardamom finish that brings to mind a refined Geisha. That’s no accident—DNA testing shows that Chiroso and Ethiopian heirloom varieties share more than just good looks.
For this lot,
Jorge
worked hard to extend the natural fermentation to 90 hours. His goals was clear, he wanted to draw out fruitiness and clarity, not funk or weight.  The result is a clean, vibrant natural coffee that doesn’t rely on process for flavor, it leans on the quality of the variety itself.
He gave it plenty of time to rest, 30 days in parchment, so it could express everything it has to offer. Roasting-wise, we started hot and kept development intentionally short to let the fruit shine and leave the cup light on its feet.
This is the kind of coffee we live for, farmer-forward, flavor-focused, rooted in excellence.

title: Buku Able Anaerobic-Guji, Ethiopia
description:
Buku Abel sits high in the Hambella area of Ethiopia’s Guji Zone, around 2,350 meters above sea level. That elevation shapes the coffee. Cool temperatures, red volcanic soil, and wide swings between day and night slow the cherries’ development, building natural sweetness and structure. Coffees from this part of Guji are expressive and fruit-forward.
This lot comes from Wondefrash, who manages the Buku Abel washing station and works closely with local smallholders. After Ethiopia changed its export regulations in 2017, he made the move from exporting to production, officially launching Buku Abel in 2019. Since then, his focus has been on consistency, not novelty especially when it comes to anaerobic fermentation.
This coffee represents Wondefrash’s third harvest refining his anaerobic process. Early experiments tested different fermentation lengths, but over time he dialed it in to what actually makes the coffee better, not louder. Today, he sticks with a 72-hour sealed anaerobic fermentation. The result: depth and sweetness without losing clarity or balance.
The variety here is 74165, a JARC selection bred for high elevations and slow, even maturation. Cherries are hand-picked at peak ripeness, carefully sorted, and sealed in oxygen-free tanks. After fermentation, the beans are slow-dried on raised beds under shade, protecting structure before resting.
In the cup, this coffee is controlled and fruit-forward. Think blueberry and raspberry notes, a jammy sweetness balanced by soft cocoa and chocolate undertones. Aromatics are vivid, but the finish stays clean. It’s expressive without ever feeling over the top a true anaerobic coffee that still tastes like coffee.
Buku Abel Anaerobics have become something of an industry favorite, and this harvest continues that trend. It’s a clear example of what happens when strong raw ingredients, high elevation, and thoughtful processing come together. This coffee knows what it’s trying to be and it does it well.
A bit about the variety: 74165 was developed by the Jimma Agricultural Research Center in the mid-1970s, during a time when coffee berry disease was putting serious pressure on farmers. The numbering simply reflects its selection history it’s not a flashy trade-named cultivar, but a locally adapted Ethiopian variety chosen for consistency and performance in the field. Think of it as a refined heirloom rather than something engineered.
JARC selected 74165 from hundreds of indigenous mother trees, prioritizing disease resistance, reliable yields, and solid cup quality. The goal wasn’t to reinvent Ethiopian coffee, just to help farmers protect what already worked. That’s why 74165 thrives in demanding high-elevation regions with high-quality potential. Today, you’ll find it across specialty lots from Guji, Yirgacheffe, Sidamo, and Jimma. Naming it isn’t a flavor promise terroir, altitude, and processing still do the heavy lifting but its track record shows that when grown and handled well, 74165 supports c

title: Seasonal Roasters Choice Subscription
description: Our Seasonal Roasters Choice subscription offers a rotating selection of our favorite single origin coffees from our seasonal collection, picked by our roasting team. These coffees are roasted to highlight the place, processing, and care given at origin. This subscription is a fantastic option for those looking to explore the variety of flavors coffee can offer without straying too far from what is familiar.

title: West Java-Sunda Coucal
description:
David Hong of Green Bean Asia is putting coffees in front of us that make me rethink some things. I’ve carried a bias against Indonesian and, honestly, a lot of Southeast Asian coffees for a long time. Too often, they’re earthy, inconsistent, or just a little tired from the way they’re traditionally handled. This one doesn’t do that. It’s floral and juicy, with fruit, chocolate, and a bright citrus snap. Crisp, creamy, and dialed in. It doesn’t just stand apart; it opens your eyes.
This lot comes from smallholder farmers in West Java working incredibly small plots, averaging just about half a hectare. These are compact shaded farms, planted in agroforestry systems where coffee grows alongside other vegetation and benefits from shade. Agroforestry supports soil health, protects water resources, increases biodiversity, and helps buffer the effects of climate change. It’s a more sustainable way to farm, but it also demands more attention and work. On farms this small, everything is hands-on, and the level of care required shows in the cup.
Instead of the more traditional wet-hulled and earthed approach, West Java-Sunda Coucal coffee is thoughtful from the start.Careful cherry selection, 84-hour anaerobic fermentation, controlled drying on raised beds. It’s clean, expressive, and shows what’s possible when producers think beyond “we’ve always done it this way” and take control of quality.
We’ve gotten to know Green Bean Asia over the past couple of years. David’s been steadily chipping away at my old assumptions, finding coffees that are thoughtful, precise, and surprising in the best possible way. This is one of those. It’s not just a great cup, it’s a reframe. A reminder that there’s a lot more going on in this part of the world than I’ve given it credit for.
More on Southeast Asian Coffee Here -
Coffee Break Ep.2 - ft. David Hong (founder of Green Bean Asia)

title: Costa Rica Las Lajas - Black Honey
description:
On the volcanic slopes of Sabanilla de Alajuela in Costa Rica's Central Valley, Las Lajas has earned a reputation as one of the country's most respected coffee producers. Oscar Chacón and Francisca Cubillo have spent decades refining their approach to cultivation and processing, helping define the quality standards that have made Costa Rican coffee a benchmark in specialty coffee.
This lot is composed of the San Isidro variety and processed using the Black Honey method, where nearly all of the fruit mucilage remains on the seed during drying. The result is a coffee that showcases both the character of the variety and the meticulous processing for which Las Lajas is known.
The cup is intensely sweet and layered, with notes of ripe berries, tropical fruit, caramelized sugar, and honey. A syrupy body carries the coffee's fruit character while maintaining clarity and balance, finishing with lasting sweetness and a refined acidity.
Every step of production, from cultivation on the volcanic soils of the Central Valley to the careful drying of the Black Honey process, contributes to a coffee that is both distinctive and approachable. It's a clear expression of producer, process, and place, one that highlights why Las Lajas remains one of the most sought-after names in Costa Rican coffee.

title: Miir Hydration Bottle
description: 20 ounce stainless steel water bottle with a screw on asymmetrical lid! Chemex drawing by a local Chicago artist on one side and our text logo on the other side. Sleek, clean and simple to get you through the approaching summer heat!

title: Kenya - Karatu SL-28
description:
In Kiambu, just north of Nairobi, mornings are cool and coffee grows slowly on small plots, usually 1–2 hectares, managed by farmers who know how to do this. This community is Gitwe Farmer Cooperative Society. Red volcanic soil, high elevation around 1850 to 1883 meters, and conditions that slow things down in the right way.
This lot is
100% SL28
, which is a bit unusual these days for Kenya. Most coffees here are blended at the farm level SL28 mixed with SL34 or newer varieties like Ruiru 11 or Batian, mainly for yield and resilience. Separating out a full SL28 lot takes more time. It’s lower yielding, more delicate, but known for its structure and acidity when it’s grown well at altitude.
At Karatu Coffee Factory, just outside Gatundu, they’ve been doing this since 1965. Eleven acres, serving four villages, Karatu, Gitwe, Kibiru, and Kigaa. Coffee grows alongside banana and maize, with grevillea and macadamia trees for shade. It’s all part of the same system.
Cherries are handpicked, focusing on ripeness. At the factory, everything is weighed and recorded before processing starts. Then it moves through depulping and into fermentation, about 72 hours, done in stages. Managed carefully to bring out clarity and structure.
After that, it’s washed and laid out on raised beds. Drying takes 7 to 15 days, depending on the weather. The pace follows the conditions.
There’s attention to the bigger picture too.
Wastewater is handled with care, and farmers are encouraged to maintain tree cover for shade and long-term stability.
It’s a coffee shaped by the consistency of people making the same careful decisions, over and over again.
What emerges reflects all of this attention to detail. Altitude gives slow flavor development. SL28 brings structure and acidity. Process brings it all together in the cup clarity.

title: Colombia
description:
The Meseta de Popayán is a high Andean plateau that sits between 1,500 and 2,070 meters above sea level.  This romantic yet functional mountain geography creates a stable climate with rich volcanic soil and a slow growing altitude.  Everything about this place is engineered by nature to grow extraordinary coffee.
Cofinet works with roughly 65 dedicated growers in this region no transactional purchasing, no chasing trends just steady, long-term partnerships. Rewarding above market prices for care, responsibility and the pride that ultimately shows up in the cup. This is how you build measurable sustainability year over year.
In the cup we find a foundational coffee.  Balanced, honest, beautifully structured.
Floral aromatics that lift out of the cup. Caramely and fudgy sweetness that anchor in the mid-palate. A soft, rounded acidity that makes it lively without ever being sharp. Clean finish. The tiniest amount of acidity.
It sits squarely in that sweet spot: refined enough for the seasoned drinker, approachable enough for someone just discovering what great coffee can be.
It performs. As espresso, it’s composed and sweet. As drip, it opens up elegant and steady. With milk, it turns into something comforting and luxurious.

title: DECAF-Palo Rosa
description:
Palo Rosa – Colombia Sugar Decaf is a coffee we’re genuinely proud to share. Grown at around 1,600 meters in the hills of Planadas, Tolima, this lot comes from the Palo Rosa Estate, where careful farming and washed processing highlight the sweetness and balance Colombia is known for. It then moves through a trusted and local supply chain, long respected for producing some of the cleanest, most consistent specialty decafs available.
This coffee is decaffeinated using the natural sugarcane (EA) process, which gently removes caffeine while keeping the character of the coffee intact. By using ethyl acetate derived from fermented sugarcane and spring water, the process preserves sweetness, structure, and clarity, so the cup still tastes like great coffee first, not “decaf.”
In the cup, Palo Rosa is smooth, comforting, and quietly complex. Expect notes of chocolate, caramelized sugar, and honey, with a soft fruit sweetness and a rounded, satisfying body. It’s the kind of decaf you can enjoy any time of day thoughtful, approachable, and crafted with the same care as our fully caffeinated offerings

title: Night Shift
description:
Night Shift isn't just a coffee—it's a nod to the ones who keep this city moving when most people are asleep. The street sweepers, the overnight nurses, the late-shift line cooks, the warehouse teams loading and unloading in the cold dark hours. The ones who aren't looking for applause. They just show up and get the job done.
That's the soul of Chicago. No frills. No excuses. Just grit, loyalty, and a good pair of boots.
This coffee is built for them.
Night Shift is a darker roast—more developed, full-bodied, and unapologetically bold. It's the kind of coffee that grabs you by the collar and gets you out the door, even when the wind off the lake is cutting through your coat. You'll taste:
Dark chocolate
Peanut butter
Caramel
Toasted marshmallow finish
We roast this coffee with intention. It's not about scorched beans or bitter endings—it's about depth. Weight. Comfort. It's a cup that holds up to cream and sugar if that's your thing, but also stands tall black. Just like the people we made it for.
Because while the city sleeps, there's a heartbeat under it all. Someone's unloading crates in a warehouse in Back of the Yards. Someone's scrubbing down a bakery kitchen in Andersonville. Someone's watching monitors in an ER in Uptown. They don't get the spotlight—but they keep the lights on.
Night Shift is for them.
It's coffee with callouses. And heart. And pride.
And it tastes damn good at 3 a.m.
Available as 12oz and 5# bags!
